blocks.title: Light dependent resistor (LDR)
blocks.text: A light dependent resistor is a resistor whose resistance decreases with increasing light intensity; because of this property it is also known as a photo resistor. LDRs are typically made from a semiconductor material like cadmium sulphide, deposited in a special pattern on an insulating plate.

The principle used in an LDR is the increase in the conductivity of the material on exposing it to light. In darkness the semiconductor material has only a few free electrons (charge carriers), resulting in high resistance. When light photons hit the material, they transfer energy to electrons in the outer orbits, making them free to conduct electricity; this decreases the resistance of the LDR. The amount of light hitting the LDR's surface determines the number of free electrons; conversely, less light results in fewer free electrons and a higher resistance. This change in resistance can be measured and used in circuits to sense light levels.

items: Light sensors: LDRs are commonly used in light-sensing circuits such as automatic lighting systems in homes and street lights; an LDR works like a switch that turns on at dusk and off at dawn.
Camera exposure control: LDRs help in adjusting the exposure time in cameras according to the amount of available light.

Voltage divider: in a typical circuit an LDR is part of a voltage divider that converts the change in resistance into a measurable change in voltage, which can be read by a microcontroller or other control circuit to act on light levels. In Fig. 9.36, in the dark the LDR has a very high resistance compared with the standard resistance (100 k ohm), so the voltage drop across the LDR, registered by a voltmeter, is very large; when the LDR is exposed to light its resistance becomes very low and the voltmeter registers a lower reading. Connecting the mid-point B to the base of an NPN transistor or to a NOT gate lets the light sensor be used as a switch.

blocks.text: Inspectors can easily check the reliability of a concrete bridge with the help of carbon fibres embedded in its slab, because carbon fibres conduct electricity (Fig. 9.37, carbon fibre sheets). Step by step:

items: Know the electrical properties of carbon fibres: they are good conductors of electricity because of their high carbon content.
Embed the carbon fibres within the slab of the concrete bridge during its construction, and connect them to form a network of conductors.
Check the reliability of the bridge by applying a small electric current to the carbon fibre network; the integrity of the concrete structure is determined by measuring the resistance of the network.

A sensor installed in the network shows whether the electric resistance is changing. If the resistance remains the same over time, the bridge is maintaining its structural integrity; if the resistance increases, the concrete is deteriorating or the carbon fibres are being damaged.

blocks.text: Other methods are also used to check the strength of a concrete bridge; for example, some sensors continuously monitor strain, vibration and temperature, and internal flaws such as cracks or voids are detected using ultrasound waves.

blocks.prompt: What is a light dependent resistor (LDR)? How can it be used as an on-off switch for lighting (comprehensive question 9.4)?
blocks.explanation: An LDR is a semiconductor (cadmium sulphide) resistor whose resistance falls as light falls on it, because photons free more electrons. In a potential divider with a fixed resistor, the voltage across the LDR is high in the dark and low in daylight; this voltage, taken to a transistor or NOT gate, switches a lamp on at dusk and off at dawn, as in automatic street lights.

items: LDR (photo resistor, cadmium sulphide): light frees electrons, so resistance falls as light intensity rises; high resistance in the dark.

Uses: automatic lights (on at dusk, off at dawn), camera exposure, potential divider with a 100 k ohm resistor driving a transistor or NOT gate. Concrete bridge: carbon fibre network; rising resistance means cracks or damaged fibres; also strain, vibration, temperature sensors and ultrasound.
